output.summary: Clump-forming perennial herb native to eastern China, Japan and Korea. Its fern-like foliage is joined in summer by tiny flowers in feathery plumes, and it naturally grows beside shaded waterways and in damp broadleaf forests.
Small annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin, Black Sea region and Macaronesia. It has thin, spreading stems, pointed leaves arranged in whorls, white flowers and smooth nutlet fruits.

Flowering plant native to Europe and Asia. Its narrow leaves resemble an ox’s tongue, while its summer flowers are small, yellow and dandelion-like; it is invasive in Africa, Australia and North America.

Fern native across broad areas of Africa, Asia, Pacific islands and eastern Australia. It can grow on other plants or on moist, well-drained ground, and its frond juice is used in Assamese traditional medicine.

Rapidly growing woody vine native to tropical dry forests from Mexico through Brazil and northern Argentina, and the Caribbean. It climbs using small aerial roots, produces yellow trumpet flowers and large underground tubers, and can spread through every forest layer.

Medium-sized tree native to the Himalayas, Tibet, southern China, Indochinese rainforests and mountainous Sumatra and Java. It has a spreading, weeping canopy and ripe fruit that may be white, pink or red and is described as honey-sweet.

Deciduous leguminous shrub native to western and central Europe. Its ridged green stems become covered with golden-yellow flowers, followed by black pods that burst open audibly and throw their seeds; it contains toxic alkaloids affecting the heart and nervous system.

Biennial or short-lived perennial native to the Andes of Argentina and Bolivia. It bears strongly night-scented, white tubular flowers above its foliage, and all parts can cause discomfort or irritation if consumed.

output.summary: Plant species in the genus Hintonia. It contains coutareagenin, described as an antidiabetic active substance.

Small epiphytic fern endemic to Terceira and Flores in the Azores and reported from Pico, where its continued existence is uncertain. It inhabits the wettest, windiest parts of moss-covered juniper rainforest, and its fronds have prominent black-edged margins. Fewer than 100 individuals are reported in the wild.

Clustering palm native to Taiwan and Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Its stems are wrapped in fine black fibres, while its fishtail-shaped leaves have silvery undersides. The fruit is reported to cause a severe allergic reaction.
output.edibilityNote: The fruit can cause a severe allergic reaction, but the exposure route and any edible preparation are not specified.

output.summary: Plant species endemic to Brazil.

Annual herb with a wide circum-Mediterranean distribution; no explicitly native origin is stated. It has simple broad leaves, and in mainland Portugal it occurs only in the Algarve on stabilized dunes and consolidated coastal sands.
Perennial herb native to central Europe. It spreads through underground stems and bears globe-shaped heads of purple to reddish flowers bordered by black or dark-brown bracts.

Large dry-season deciduous or semi-evergreen tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina. Its heart-shaped leaves have notably extended tips, and the tree is sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and Jainism.

Evergreen tree native to the subtropical mountains of southern China and Taiwan. It has glossy, feathery foliage and fragrant white trumpet-shaped flowers that open at night and wilt the following morning.

Soft-wooded shrub native to eastern Australia; in New Zealand it is reported as indigenous, though some authorities consider it introduced. It has blue-purple flowers and orange-red to scarlet fruit. Ripe berries were traditional Māori food and were stewed or made into pies and jam by early European settlers; using leaves in hāngī is now discouraged because they contain poisonous alkaloids.

output.summary: Annual herb native from Europe and Macaronesia east to Assam. It is densely hairy near the stem tops and sepals, with small white flowers packed into tight clusters. Its leaves and shoots were wild food in ancient China, and the leaves can be boiled and eaten.
output.edibilityNote: Leaves and shoots were eaten as wild food in ancient China; the leaves can be boiled and eaten.

output.summary: Aromatic shrub endemic to Mexico. It bears rounded, lobed leaves and yellow flower clusters, blooming in the dry season, roughly November to March.

Annual flowering herb native to Eurasia. Its square stems carry leaves that shade from green below to purple above, and unlike true nettles it cannot sting. Young tops and leaves are eaten in salads, stir-fries or sauces, while flowers can be crystallized with sugar and egg white.
output.edibilityNote: Young tops and leaves are used in salads, stir-fries or sauces; flowers can be crystallized with sugar and egg white.

output.summary: Annual or biennial herb native to Europe. Its erect stem and divided leaves are hairy, while its yellow flowers usually have five petals and five sepals bent backward. It favors moist, disturbed places and is introduced in areas including parts of the United States and Australia.

Deciduous shrub or small tree native to southern China and southern Japan. It typically grows in scrubland and woodland, and its accepted Japanese and Chinese varieties occupy the corresponding parts of its native range.

Perennial sedge with no native origin specified in the supplied information. It is widespread across tropical and subtropical regions, favoring brackish water and other saline or alkaline wetlands. It can form rhizome-linked clumps and bears cylindrical spikelets ranging from green to reddish or dark brown.
Plant native to Europe from Portugal to Ukraine. Known as waxy bedstraw, it is only sparingly naturalized in a few locations in Quebec, Ontario, Connecticut and New Jersey.

Annual flowering herb native to the Palaearctic. Its small yellow flower heads usually lack ray florets, with the disc florets mostly hidden by black-tipped bracts. It thrives in disturbed ground and reseeds from downy seeds that become sticky when wet.
output.edibilityNote: Reported as poisonous to humans; chronic exposure to its pyrrolizidine alkaloids can cause irreversible liver damage.

output.summary: Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

Juniper shrub native to the mountains of central and southern Europe and western and central Asia. Mature plants carry scale-like leaves, sometimes retaining juvenile needle-like leaves, especially on shaded lower shoots. Its berry-like cones are blue-black with a whitish waxy coating.
output.edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous because they contain toxic compounds, including ethereal oils.

output.summary: Deciduous shrub native to China, Japan and South Korea. It grows on sunny, forested slopes and has a repeating leaf-angle pattern of 180°, 90°, 180° and 270°.

Bulbous perennial endemic to Morocco and Portugal, although Moroccan plants have often been confused with a distinct species. This dwarf bluebell has long, narrow leaves and blue, violet or white bell- or star-shaped flowers in spring. It grows in damp, often sandy open ground near sea level.

A perennial herb native to the eastern and central United States, violet woodsorrel grows from an underground bulb and has three heart-shaped leaflets and lavender-to-white spring flowers. All parts are edible and used in salads, but only moderate amounts are advised because its oxalic acid can be poisonous in large quantities.

output.summary: A herbaceous perennial with a broadly Mediterranean distribution, prostrate Canary clover has woody stems, five-part hairy leaves and clusters of small white flowers. Its fruits are reddish-brown pods containing one or two seeds.

An evergreen tree endemic to New Zealand, tarata has yellow-green, curly-edged leaves that smell strongly of lemon when crushed. Fragrant yellow-cream spring flowers are followed by black seed capsules, and young conical trees become rounded as they mature.
A daffodil native to the central Iberian Peninsula, Narcissus rupicola grows on rocky ledges and in crevices with very little soil.
A flowering plant native to Western Europe.

A herbaceous perennial native to El Salvador, Peru, Bolivia, Colombia, Venezuela, Costa Rica and Ecuador, and naturalized in Puerto Rico, hanging lobster claw grows in tropical rainforests. Its hanging flower clusters have downward-facing bracts, with the flowers tucked beneath them.
A flowering plant whose two listed subspecies are native to mainland Portugal.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to eastern Asia, specifically central and southern Japan and Taiwan, holly olive bears very fragrant white flowers in autumn. Spiny leaves predominate on young plants, while unspined leaves predominate higher on mature plants; dark purple fruit ripens the following summer.

An evergreen flowering plant of unknown original range, ti is believed native from Bangladesh through Southeast Asia, southern China and Taiwan to New Guinea and northern Australia. Its palm-like form carries fan-like clusters of green, red or variegated leaves. Roots and young leaves can be cooked as survival food, while Polynesian green forms supply processed sweet rhizomes and Hawaiian roots can be fermented and distilled.

output.summary: An annual herb probably native to Central America, jimsonweed has night-opening trumpet-shaped flowers and egg-shaped seed capsules that may be spiny. It is poisonous: all parts contain dangerous tropane alkaloids, and ingestion can cause delirium, hallucinations and potentially fatal poisoning.
output.edibilityNote: All parts contain dangerous tropane alkaloids; ingestion can cause severe poisoning and carries a high risk of fatal overdose.

output.summary: A unicellular green microalga found worldwide in freshwater and terrestrial habitats, it has spherical cells with a pea-green, cup-shaped chloroplast. Since the 1990s it has been considered a protein-rich food source and is now sold internationally as a dietary supplement or food additive.

output.summary: A large shrub or small tree endemic to southern and eastern South Africa and neighbouring territories such as Eswatini, it bears abundant, extremely fragrant flowers with long tubes accessible only to nocturnal hawkmoths. Its hard, woody fruit can remain on the tree for years if large browsers or elephants do not eat it.

A large shrub or tree native to mountains of the western Mediterranean, from southern France through Spain to Morocco and locally northern Algeria, it has strongly aromatic, spicy-resinous foliage. Male and female plants are separate, and its cones are berry-like, blue-black and waxy, maturing in about 18 months.
A conifer tree endemic to Norfolk Island, it is not a true pine and has a straight trunk with regularly layered, symmetrical branches. Its mature cones break apart to release nut-like edible seeds.

output.summary: A flowering plant in the mustard family, it has flowers visited by many types of insects.

An annual herb in the mustard family, it forms a basal leaf rosette and flowering stems that may have leaves or be leafless. In western Europe it blooms from June through October, while elsewhere in its range flowering may extend for up to eight months.

A herbaceous perennial native to the Caucasus, Turkey and northern Iran, it has aromatic leaves and violet or lilac-blue summer flowers. Like other catmints, it can produce a euphoric effect in some domestic cats.
A small perennial herb native to Europe, North Africa and parts of western Asia including Turkey, it has a self-supporting habit and simple, broad leaves.

A climbing flowering plant native to Taiwan and Japan’s Ryukyu Islands, it produces smooth, round leaves and tiny white flowers. It is not particularly rare in Taiwan but is listed as critically endangered in Japan.
A lily-family plant native to Mediterranean areas of Spain, France, Sardinia, Sicily and Algeria, including the Balearic Islands and Corsica.
